newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Row over Ramos term revives Marcos ghost.
newsitem.headline: Row over Ramos term revives Marcos ghost.

text.p: A move to extend Philippine President Fidel Ramos's term has divided a nation he vowed to unify, alarmed big business and set the government on a collision course with the powerful Roman Catholic Church, analysts say.
The row has also clouded this week's commemoration of the 1986 "people power" revolt that ended Ferdinand Marcos's rule and restored democracy to this fractious nation.

Opposition parties last week signed a compact to launch nationwide protests, warning Ramos he was "inviting a cataclysm". Leftists are organising rallies and businessmen who took part in the anti-Marcos uprising have threatened to march.

"Surely, President Ramos ... would not wish his achievements drowned in a spittle of national contempt," the newspaper Today said in an editorial on proposals to amend the constitution so that Ramos can remain in power after his term ends in June 1998.

Church sources said they expected Cardinal Jaime Sin, the country's leading prelate, to lambast the term extension moves in a homily he will deliver at a mass on Tuesday commemorating the 1986 revolt.
It was Sin who rallied a million Filipinos to gather on Manila's Edsa highway and protect army mutineers, led by Ramos and then defence chief Juan Ponce Enrile, from advancing Marcos tanks.
"The embers of Edsa are being stoked into a flame again, and may turn into a raging fire before long," the Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper said in an editorial on Sunday.
"The call for a charter change has brought in its train a louder call for the people to come together, as they once did at Edsa, to fight an oppression, to end an inequity," it added.

Ramos has said he will step down next year in line with a constitutional provision fixing a president's term at six years without re-election -- a limitation designed to curb ambitions by anyone to follow the path of Marcos's authoritarian rule.
Newspapers questioned Ramos's sincerity after members of his Lakas (People Power) party said that they favoured lifting term limits and that they believed they could convince the president.
A simultaneous campaign by a citizens' group to gather five million signatures to force the holding of a plebiscite to amend the charter has deepened public scepticism.
"President Ramos ought to know better than imperilling economic growth ... by introducing a new element of instability at this point," the Malaya (Free) newspaper said.
Ramos has won wide praise for turning the country into a vibrant economy by liberalising the banking, oil and telecommunications sectors.

Many political analysts view the signature campaign and calls by Ramos's aides for constitutional changes -- officially disowned by him -- as part of an administration ploy to test the waters and see how far the idea of a second term would go.
The strategy, they said, is premised on official perception that opposition to a term extension is based largely in urban centres and fuelled by politicians aspiring to succeed him.
"Ramos is a poker player. He will push if it is possible, and wait to see how the situation develops," said Alex Magno, political science professor at the University of the Philippines.
"The danger, if he steps too fast too far ahead, is political defeat, loss of face, as he nears the end of his term."
Former president Corazon Aquino, who helped lead the Edsa revolt, has vowed to lead street protests if needed.
Analysts said, however, that if opposition to charter change became too formidable, Ramos would step back and endorse a candidate of his choice.
His perceived statesmanship would then ensure his candidate's victory and he would, by then, also have wrecked the campaign timetables of other presidential dreamers, they said.
